items.title: You can’t eliminate uncertainty — but you can prevent it from paralyzing you
items.description:
At the time of this writing, there is no consensus about how COVID started.  
 My colleagues and I tried to harness that uncertainty as a strength. Rather than waiting for certainty to arrive, we began acting in its absence. Not knowing the origins of COVID meant we were forced — as we readied the country and world for future unknown threats — to make ourselves safer from all potential causes: natural spillovers, lab accidents, and biological weapons. items.title: Mapped: Every known (and suspected) road in the Roman Empire
items.description:
Rome wasn’t built in a day .  All roads lead to Rome . A recent study now links those two well-worn proverbs by suggesting that the footprint of Roman road infrastructure was 59% larger than previously thought. The revelation isn’t just quantitative — a network with a finer mesh might change what we think life was like across Rome’s vast domain.

items.description: Out there in the Universe, there are some incredibly impressive astrophysical entities, including behemoths that dwarf anything we’re familiar with. There are stars hundreds of times more massive, and millions of times as luminous, as our own Sun is. There are galaxies and galaxy clusters thousands of times as massive as our Milky Way and Local Group. items.title: Cosmology’s oldest question: How the universe will end
items.description:
By the end of the 20th century, physicists believed they had answered one of cosmology’s oldest questions: the universe would expand forever, its galaxies drifting into isolation until only our immediate neighborhood remained. Astrophysicist Ethan Siegel explains how that conclusion was reached. Now new measurements of galaxies across vast stretches of cosmic time suggest dark energy may not be constant after all.

items.title: AI is forcing us to reckon with a 400-year-old problem
items.description: Like much modern fantasy, Philip Pullman’s  His Dark Materials  series features magical objects. Each book in the trilogy is named after one; the second is  The Subtle Knife . This knife looks unremarkable, but when wielded by the right person, it can cut a hole in the world — a portal into an alternate universe. items.title: A psychologist’s guide to understanding and spotting narcissism
items.description:
Narcissistic people are often charming at the dinner party and cruel in the car ride home, which tells you they can control it. Clinical psychologist Ramani Durvasula, author of It’s Not You, has studied narcissism since long before it became a buzzword, and she argues that most of what circulates online gets it wrong. 
 This video  A psychologist’s guide to understanding and spotting narcissism  is featured on  Big Think .

items.title: 10 perspectives that divide the AI world
items.description:

items.description:

items.title: Made in Our Image
items.description: In the output of AI, we see ourselves refracted through a strange new form of intelligence. This issue is an attempt to make sense of those refractions.

items.title: The sci-fi inspired “cloaking device” makes invisibility possible
